mappings.note: Counts the siblings named in the story. Single-fact retrieval, LO-1.
What the seagull feared is his defining state of mind, so LO-2, matching the other items about his fear.
Lack of courage is a character trait rather than a narrated event, so LO-2 rather than LO-1.
How long he was left alone is a stated figure; retrieval, LO-1.
The text says outright that he felt the heat because he had not eaten; the cause is extracted, not inferred, so LO-1.
Which family member watched him is a stated detail; retrieval, LO-1.
Reproduces the exact cry quoted in the story ('Ga, ga, ga'). Extraction, LO-1.
The pretence of falling asleep is narrated; retrieval, LO-1. The 'why did he pretend' version is the LO-2 item.
'Exhausted by the strange exercise' is the story's own phrase, so the cause is retrieved rather than argued; LO-1.
Places the flight on Maslow's hierarchy and asks the learner to justify the placement - reasoning from an outside framework, C-E1.2, not extraction from the text.
Judging which parenting style the seagull's parents show is character analysis (LO-2), argued as the learner's own attribution against a given typology (C-E1.2).
'Justify this statement by taking points from the lesson' demands textual evidence, which is LO-3; C-E1.2 would fit only if the support came from outside the text.
The landing and floating on the sea are narrated step by step; information extraction, LO-1.
How he overcame fear and then showed joy traces his emotional arc - character, LO-2.
Lists the family's tactics (calls, taunts, threats, the fish). Narrated detail, LO-1, while the 'what was the mother's plan' item is LO-2.
Three of the four parts retrieve stated facts from the extract (LO-1); the last asks which word means 'eat quickly', a vocabulary item (C-E1.1).
Lead part rules out a wrong gloss for 'pretended' (vocabulary, C-E1.1); the longer part asks why the family deliberately ignored him, which is motive (LO-2).
Both parts read behind the action - what the mother's derisive scream shows about her impatience, and why the chick was overjoyed. Motive and feeling, LO-2.
'When' did he get over the fear is answered by the narrated sequence of the first flight; retrieval, LO-1.
Describes his reaction (a joyful scream, leaning out eagerly) - his feeling at that moment, LO-2.
The family's celebration is narrated in the closing paragraph; retrieval, LO-1.
Why he stayed behind is his fear that his wings would not hold him - a state of mind, LO-2.
Contrasting the seagull at the start and at the end is a character arc, LO-2, not a list of events.
Invent a conversation between the siblings. Dialogue composition in a given register - C-E1.2.
Tests Richard Bach's claim against what the story shows about this gull, so the answer must be built on textual evidence (LO-3) rather than personal preference (C-E1.2).
In 'The Black Aeroplane', identifying the risk and why the pilot accepts it is about his motive and judgement, LO-2.
Describes what happened once the Dakota entered the storm - narrated events, LO-1.
'Mention any two traits supported by the textual evidence' is the explicit evidence requirement of LO-3; LO-2 alone would not force the citation.
What passed through his mind on calling Paris Control is narrated (breakfast, the holiday); retrieval, LO-1.
Lists the failures in the storm - dead compass, dead radio, no reply. Extraction, LO-1.
What kept troubling him afterwards is the unresolved mystery in his mind, so his state of mind, LO-2, rather than a retrievable event.
The woman's reason - no second plane on the radar - is stated in the closing lines; retrieval, LO-1.
Near-duplicate of the previous item and answered by the same stated fact, so the same retrieval outcome.
What the narrator felt on the calm flight home - contentment, anticipation - is his inner state, LO-2.
Time and manner of the first radio call are stated (one-thirty, the Dakota DS 088 message); retrieval, LO-1.
The instruction to turn twelve degrees west and what he then did are narrated; extraction, LO-1.
The black aeroplane with no lights on its wings is described in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
How he escaped the clouds - by following the other aircraft - is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
A malformed duplicate whose question field has swallowed the previous item's answer, but the question it asks is the same escape-from-the-clouds retrieval, LO-1.
Picks the words that mean roughly the same as 'fly' from a long list. Vocabulary and shades of meaning, C-E1.1.
